In summary, our research is concerned with
the repair and recombination of DNA damage induced by UV‐irradiation in Haemophilus.
the role of recA protein in the repair of UV damage in H. influenzae.
the study of recombination repair of ultraviolet‐irradiation damage in Haemophilus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in Haemophilus, the repair of ultraviolet‐irradiation inactivation of transforming DNA is due to recombination.
in the presence of a functional RecA gene product, recombination repair can repair UV‐induced damage to transforming DNA, but excision repair is not involved.
the recA4 mutation is responsible for the observed deficiency in recombination‐mediated repair of ultraviolet‐irradiation‐induced lesions in the DNA of Haemophilis influenzae.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the repair of transforming DNA by recombination repair in H. influenzae strain Rd is not dependent on the presence of the recA gene product.
the recA‐dependent recombination repair is the major pathway for the repair of ultraviolet‐irradiation‐induced DNA damage in H. influenzae.
inactivation kinetics are determined by the relative rates of recombination and excision repair, and the shape of the curves depends on the relative rates of these two repair mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, at least in Haemophilus, excision repair is not required for recombination repair to occur.
recombination repair can be demonstrated in Haemophilus and that it is the predominant repair mechanism in this organism.
